messages.content: Help me extract all data entries with the attribute 'data-active' set to true from a list element stored in a variable named 'listElement'?

function.name: getActiveDataEntries
function.description: This function extracts data entries from a list element based on a specified attribute and its value. It checks for the presence of the 'data-active' attribute and whether it is set to true. Note that the provided function is in JavaScript syntax.

listElement.description: The list element from which to extract active data entries. This parameter can be of any type of JavaScript object in string representation.

attribute.description: The data attribute used to filter entries. Optional parameter with a default value of 'data-active'. This is JavaScript String type parameter in string representation.

value.description: The value of the attribute to match. Optional parameter with a default value of true. This is JavaScript Boolean type parameter in string representation.

message.content:
Sure thing!  
If you already have a list element stored in a variable called `listElement`, you can pull out every entry that has `data-active="true"` with a single call to the helper function.

```javascript
// Assuming `listElement` is a JavaScript object (e.g., an array of items)
// that contains a `data-active` attribute on each entry.
const activeEntries = getActiveDataEntries({
  listElement: listElement,   // <-- your list element
  attribute: 'data-active',   // optional – defaults to 'data-active'
  value: true                 // optional – defaults to true
});

console.log(activeEntries);   // array of entries where data-active === true
```

### Using the tool directly

If you want to invoke the tool straight away (for example, in a notebook or a script that supports the `functions.getActiveDataEntries` call), you can do it like this:

```json
{
  "listElement": "listElement",
  "attribute": "data-active",
  "value": "true"
}
```

> **Note:**  
> Replace `"listElement"` with the *actual string representation* of your list element (e.g., `JSON.stringify(listElement)` if it’s an object). The tool expects the list element to be passed as a string, so if you’re calling it from JavaScript you can just pass the variable itself; if you’re calling it from another environment you’ll need to serialize it first.

That’s all you need—now you’ll get back an array of all the active entries!
